articles.title_orig: Trump, Xi and Putin plan an unprecedented joint meeting on the sidelines of APEC, officials say
articles.title_zh: Trump, Xi and Putin plan an unprecedented joint meeting on the sidelines of APEC, officials say
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — The leaders of the United States, China and Russia plan to meet Thursday on the sidelines of next week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China’s tech hub of Shenzhen — an unprecedented gathering of the heads of the world’s biggest nuclear powers.
While the leaders gathering for joint talks will mark a singular moment, analysts say expectations are low that the talks will lead to major breakthroughs and say they will be heavier in symbolism than substance.
Plans for the three-way summit with Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin were confirmed on Friday by the White House. It comes at a complicated moment in relations between the three countries.
Trump has warmly embraced Xi after coming to a truce in their short-lived trade war last year and in spite of differences over the U.S. war with Iran and other tensions between the world’s foremost economic powers.
Similarly, Trump has sought to build his relationship with Putin, even as the Russian leader has persisted in his nearly 5-year-old war with Ukraine and as Moscow has deepened its military, intelligence and diplomatic partnership with Iran.
The U.S. president has insisted that such a meeting would provide an opportunity for the three leaders to discuss the U.S. war with Iran and his goal of reaching a three-way agreement on their nuclear arms stockpiles.
The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States expired in February, removing caps on the two largest atomic arsenals for the first time in more than a half-century. When that treaty — known as New START — expired, Trump rejected a call by Russia to extend the two-country deal for another year and called for “a new, improved and modernized” deal that includes China.
The trilateral meeting is expected to serve as a start to the nuclear talks between the three leaders and no agreements are expected to be announced, according to a senior U.S. official who briefed reporters on the condition of anonymity.
But Beijing’s arsenal of more than 600 warheads, according to Pentagon estimates, is far smaller than inventories held by the U.S. and Russia, each estimated to have more than 5,000 warheads. With U.S. and Russian arsenals dwarfing its stockpile, China has shown little interest in developing a nuclear pact.
By agreeing to host the meeting, Xi may be calculating that the moment offers him an opportunity to flex China’s growing clout and prestige.
For the Kremlin, the planned trilateral meeting is a coveted chance to posture as a superpower on par with Washington and Beijing.
“I think the key for Putin was that this was very much about signaling a desire to talk to the president and talk to Chairman Xi in a way that suggests that they’re making decisions on Ukraine, which obviously the Ukrainians and the Europeans don’t like,” said Edgard Kagan, a former U.S. ambassador to Malaysia who is now at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
The trilateral could very well overshadow the APEC summit. The summit, which is bringing 21 economies to Shenzhen, marks a big moment for China to show off its fast-growing, ultramodern coastal metropolis that transformed from a small fishing village into a global technology and economic hub in just a few decades.
More substantively, such a gathering could also muddy China’s argument that a Cold War mentality in the West was a contributing factor that led to Russia’s war on Ukraine and its pointed criticism that the U.S. has undermined international institutions and treaties with how it has executed its war against Iran.
The trilateral meeting could undercut China’s push to portray itself as a defender of free trade at APEC, said Hoo Tiang Boon, a professor of Chinese foreign policy at Nanyang Technological University.
“You sort of run counter to Chinese support of multilateralism,” he said.
Putin and Xi are no strangers. They’ve fostered a close personal relationship, meeting more than 40 times since Xi became president in 2013 and addressing each other as “dear friend.”
Trump and Putin have met face-to-face on seven different occasions, most recently in Alaska in August 2025. Xi and Trump have held face-to-face talks on eight occasions, including a September state visit to Washington by Xi.
Beijing is the No. 1 trading partner for Moscow, a relationship that has strengthened since Putin sent troops into Ukraine in 2022.
As the EU and the West sought to economically isolate Russia, China increased its purchases of Russia’s energy resources and became Moscow’s principal supplier of key technologies, including high-tech components for Russian weapons industries. Beijing has ignored Western demands to cut those supplies.
In the lead-up to Russia’s war on Ukraine, Xi and Putin declared their countries had a “no-limits friendship.” China officially has said it is neutral on the conflict, while charging that Kyiv’s Western allies played a part in provoking Russia’s military action in Ukraine.
Moscow, in turn, has repeatedly declared its support for Beijing’s policy on issues related to Taiwan.
Trump recently struck a diesel deal with Russia, waiving sanctions against Moscow and allowing for the sale of millions of tons of the fuel. The U.S. leader has blamed surging energy prices on Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil refineries. Analysts, however, say the rise in global crude prices is due mostly to the Iran war.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has expressed concern that the trilateral meeting could serve as a platform for discussing a possible Ukraine deal behind Kyiv’s back.
Planning for the summit has drawn comparisons to the Yalta Conference, the 1945 gathering at which the leaders of the U.S., Britain and the Soviet Union agreed to divide Germany and Berlin into four military occupation zones and finalized plans for establishing the United Nations.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has dismissed the Yalta comparisons, noting that any potential agreements reached in Shenzhen can’t be enforced on others.
“It’s clear that a meeting between the leaders of countries such as Russia, China and the United States is extremely significant,” Peskov said. “However, let’s not forget that the vision for a global order is that no one tries to impose any particular view of global order, and it should be based entirely on mutual benefit and mutual respect.”

articles.title_orig: Afghanistan’s new road to China ends at a closed border
articles.title_zh: Afghanistan’s new road to China ends at a closed border
articles.content_orig:
At an altitude of nearly 4,900 metres, at the Wakhjir Pass, Afghanistan ends and China begins. Snow closes the pass for at least five months of the year, and people cross it only sporadically in the months when it is passable.
There is no official border crossing here, and yet, on October 4, Afghanistan’s Taliban-led government celebrated the opening of a road leading to the frontier – but crucially not crossing it.
Afghanistan’s Ministry of Rural Rehabilitation and Development said the road through the Wakhan Corridor in Badakhshan province had been built in two phases for 365 million afghanis ($5.5m).
It is a basic road – an unpaved track covered with gravel. On the other side of the border, there is no Chinese customs facility, and China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has not commented on the road’s opening.
For the moment, the road leads to a closed border, with no indication of when Beijing might open it to commercial traffic.
The Wakhan Corridor is a narrow protruding stretch of land extending for about 350 kilometres (220 miles). It lies between Tajikistan to the north and Pakistan to the south, but is entirely within Afghan territory, connecting it with China.
The corridor’s unusual shape was determined by the competition between Britain and Russia over the region in the 19th century. An agreement between the two powers in 1895 delineated Afghanistan’s northern boundary with Russian territories (that now make up modern-day Tajikistan), and left Wakhan under Kabul’s control to separate the Russian-controlled land from British India.
China was not a party to the conflict, however, and Kabul and Beijing did not settle the border until 1963.
The area – on both sides of the border – is remote. But in recent years it has gradually become one of Asia’s most sensitive geopolitical crossroads, where China’s security concerns, Afghanistan’s economic ambitions, the interests of Pakistan and Iran, and Central Asian countries’ regional connectivity projects intersect.
As competition intensifies over trade and logistics routes across Asia, this narrow corridor could take on a role far beyond its geographical limits: a potential link between South, East and Central Asia, and a key to reshaping patterns of trade and influence in the region.
Serious discussion of a road through Wakhan began in June 2009, during discussions between the Afghan and Chinese governments.
However, the project went no further than preliminary studies at the time, with the corridor’s rugged terrain cited as a major obstacle to implementation.
The Chinese press at the time also noted concerns over national security, particularly that Uighur fighters could use the corridor as an entry point into China.
The project was frozen until 2019, when Afghanistan began building a road in Wakhan, according to former Afghan ambassador to China, Javid Qaem.
Sixty kilometres (37 miles) were completed, “but the sudden change of government in Afghanistan in August 2021 led to the plan being postponed”, Qaem told Al Jazeera, in reference to the Taliban takeover.
Former Afghan acting defence minister, Shah Mahmoud Miakhel, who served in the position in 2021 and left a few months before the Taliban took power, told Al Jazeera that “the presence of [United States] and foreign forces and the security situation” prevented the road project from being implemented.
“Beijing considered those circumstances to be limiting the prospects for developing the corridor,” Miakhel said.
The Taliban government, however, picked up the project in the years since, making it one of its strategic projects while strengthening political and diplomatic contacts with Beijing.
It hopes to turn the corridor from an isolated border area into a gateway connecting Afghanistan to Chinese and Central Asian markets and strengthening its position in regional trade networks.
“The Taliban resumed construction of the Wakhan road in September 2023, seeking financial support from China to build this future trade route, but China has not yet agreed to open its border with Afghanistan because of security threats,” Qaem said.
In January 2024, the Taliban announced that the road had reached the Chinese border. In March 2025, the rural development ministry signed a contract with local companies for a second, 71-kilometre (44-mile) phase. The authorities say the project was funded from Afghan government resources, and the available information does not indicate any Chinese funding.
In August 2025, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi – the most senior Chinese official to visit Afghanistan since the Taliban returned to power – made his second visit to Kabul since the takeover.
In his meeting with Afghan Interior Minister Sirajuddin Haqqani, Wang said China “supports the early resumption of bilateral patrols in the Wakhan Corridor to maintain peace and tranquillity in the border areas”. He also called on Kabul to crack down on the East Turkestan Islamic Movement, a Uighur separatist group.
Unlike Afghanistan, China does not view the Wakhan Corridor primarily as an economic project, but as a highly sensitive security issue. Beijing’s priorities in Afghanistan fall into three main areas: protecting its western border, preventing armed groups from entering Xinjiang (East Turkestan), and safeguarding its investments in natural resources, as well as protecting the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor.
An Afghan government source, who requested anonymity, offered Kabul’s account of China’s position.
“China does not oppose opening its border with Afghanistan through the Wakhan Corridor, but it links implementation of the project to the availability of effective security guarantees,” the source told Al Jazeera. The source said that the Taliban had demonstrated their ability to maintain security and secure the border.
The question of Xinjiang, considered by the Uighur people to be their homeland, is therefore the apparent priority for China when it comes to Wakhan.
A 2022 United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights report condemned the “arbitrary detention of Uighurs and other Muslims in Xinjiang”. China has rejected the findings, describing them as part of a Western campaign against it.
Beijing continues to proceed cautiously when it comes to Afghanistan. Major Chinese investments have stalled. In June 2025, the Taliban cancelled an oil exploration contract in the Amu Darya Basin with a Chinese company, saying it had failed to fulfil its obligations. And in May of this year, Afghanistan’s mining minister complained to the Chinese ambassador about delays in the Mes Aynak copper mine project, which has yet to begin production.
China shares land borders with 14 countries and maintains extensive economic and trade relations with most of its neighbours. But Afghanistan, alongside Bhutan, remain the only countries bordering China that have yet to benefit from a direct overland crossing for trade.
Kabul wants Wakhan to provide a route that is not controlled by Islamabad. Afghanistan is landlocked, and its routes to the sea run through Pakistan and Iran. Over the past year, both routes have been all but closed at the same time.
Mohammad Ismail Ghaznawi, who was governor of Badakhshan before becoming deputy minister of public works for road maintenance in August, said the Wakhan road project was “part of the government’s plan to diversify trade outlets and reduce dependence on Pakistani border crossings”, and referenced fighting between Afghan and Pakistani forces that has been ongoing this year.
Ghaznawi added that the US-Israel war on Iran also directly affects Afghan trade, making the opening of alternative routes a priority.
The Afghan government views the road as the beginning of a trade corridor, and perhaps a railway in the future, that would connect the country to China’s Belt and Road Initiative and generate transit fees.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang Resigns, Leaving Nvidia’s China Chip Fight Without Its Chief Advocate
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang Resigns, Leaving Nvidia’s China Chip Fight Without Its Chief Advocate
articles.content_orig:

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned from his top post at the chipmaker he co-founded, after reports of the tech titan's extramarital affairs came into the spotlight this week.
One of those relationships has raised national security concerns. The New York Times reported that Huang had an affair with a businesswoman U.S. intelligence suspects to be a Chinese spy, which Beijing denies. Separately, the outlet and later others reported that Nvidia employees said Huang had another affair with an executive who reported to him directly — compounding calls for him to step down.
Nvidia announced Huang's resignation on Thursday, effective immediately. The California-based company said that Colette Kress — who has been Nvidia's chief financial officer and executive vice president since 2013 — will step into the role of interim CEO.
The scandal marks the most tumultuous chapter yet for Nvidia, whose high-end chips have emerged as the leading building blocks for artificial intelligence. Huang himself has become a key face in the AI race, both across the industry and often on U.S. President Donald Trump’s side in Washington.
Nvidia said Kress is now interim CEO. Prior to joining Nvidia over 13 years ago, Kress worked at Cisco, Microsoft and Texas Instruments.
In a statement about her new post on Thursday, Kress said Nvidia’s “strength has always come from its people” and that she's “committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years.”
Huang co-founded Nvidia, alongside Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, back in 1993 — and until Thursday had led the company ever since, with no clear successor in sight. Huang's ouster has led to a scramble for a new permanent CEO, and Nvidia said it's considering both “internal and external candidates.”
The company's board of directors also said Thursday that it has named its first-ever chairman, Harvey C. Jones.
Over the weekend, following news reports of Huang's relationship with a woman identified as former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, Nvidia's then-CEO apologized for being “unfaithful to my wife.”
"My actions hurt her and our children,” Huang wrote in a Sunday email to employees, adding that his colleagues also “deserve better” from him.
Neither Huang nor Nvidia identified who he had been intimate with by name, but the apology arrived shortly after Nvidia said it was investigating whether Huang had been “the target of a foreign intelligence effort.”
Last month, the Times reported that U.S. intelligence agencies discovered Nvidia’s Huang had developed a close relationship with Alice Huang, who also goes by the name Huang Le — and determined she was feeding information directly to Beijing. (Huang is a common surname and the two are not related).
Nvidia initially maintained Huang would stay on as CEO as the company conducted its investigation. But scrutiny grew late Wednesday after reports emerged that Huang had a separate affair with an Nvidia executive. Huang’s resignation arrived shortly after. The company didn't address either relationship in its Thursday announcement.
Later on Thursday, Reuters reported Huang had an intimate relationship with a second employee, citing unidentified sources.
Where investigations stand
Nvidia hasn't provided any notable new updates in its internal review announced Sunday. At the time, the company said it had “no reason to believe” that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, but that its inquiry would examine all available information.
Trump was reportedly briefed about intelligence findings involving Huang well before the scandal erupted publicly. But when asked over the weekend whether he wished he had acted sooner on that information, the president said “I don’t think so” and maintained that Nvidia’s CEO was an “honorable guy.”
Trump later said the FBI is looking into Huang's affair with Alice Huang, although where exactly that probe stands is unclear. Meanwhile, lawmakers from both sides of the aisle on Capitol Hill are calling for further investigations.
Many eyes have been on Nvidia’s ties to Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which prominently touts the companies’ partnership on its website. Last year, Megaspeed was accused of illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China, but in December said there was “no evidence” of such exports.
On Thursday, Megaspeed maintained it takes its obligation to comply with American export control laws “extremely seriously" — and that it was committed to working “constructively and transparently” with the U.S. government.
Singaporean authorities said they questioned Alice Huang and confiscated her passport last year as part of an investigation into Megaspeed. They concluded there wasn’t enough evidence that she had committed a crime, but suspected she provided “inaccurate information” to downplay her role at Megaspeed.
Malaysia said Friday it was investigating whether any of the chips brought into Malaysia by Megaspeed or its Malaysian affiliate Speedmatrix had been reexported to other country.
China, meanwhile, has denied that it attempted to ensnare Jensen Huang. Its Foreign Ministry earlier this week called the spying allegations “unsubstantiated” and said they amount to a smear campaign against Beijing.
Trump continues his praise for Huang
Huang has maintained a close relationship to Trump throughout the Republican president’s second term in office. He’s successfully lobbied for looser AI regulation overall — including less strict limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China. And he's among tech CEOs who have dined at the White House, and even traveled on Air Force One.
Trump has called Huang “smart” and “amazing,” repeatedly insisting he join him on foreign trips. After news of his resignation broke on Thursday, the president maintained that Huang had “done a fantastic job.”
He also chimed in with his own recommendation for Nvidia's CEO seat: former chief executive of Apple Tim Cook, who has similarly remained in Trump's orbit over recent years.
“There is only one man to take his place,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform Thursday. “Legend replaces a Legend!”
Critics quickly decried Trump's comments. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said the Republican administration had “repeatedly undermined the free market economy” and that Thursday marked the latest example of “ Donald Trump weighing in on behalf of his views connected to corporate America, as opposed to focusing on working class America.”
A new test for the AI industry
The shockwaves of Huang's exit stress just how few figures hold so much power the AI race. Nvidia is one of the world’s most valuable companies today — and Huang himself (often wearing his signature leather jacket) has risen to fame across the tech world.
Some analysts suspect the foreign intelligence allegations will strengthen calls in Washington for stricter export controls with China, which could in turn renew trade strains overall. Others have called it a watershed moment for Nvidia, the chipmaker that has long been seen as the crown jewel for powering AI. And questions of security risks facing the companies at the forefront of this technology are piling up.
Nvidia shares fell more than 4% by market close Thursday, after plummeting earlier in the day.
Stephanie Balaouras, group research director for Forrester, said Huang’s resignation from Nvidia isn’t just a test for the company but the AI boom as a whole.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX Starship Flight 15 live updates: Starship enters orbit on 22-hour flight after launch success
articles.title_zh: SpaceX Starship Flight 15 live updates: Starship enters orbit on 22-hour flight after launch success
articles.content_orig:
Flight 15 expected to orbit Earth about 14 times over 22 hours, before company catches it at Starbase, Texas
SpaceX’s Starship megarocket blasted off from Texas on Friday afternoon, as the aerospace company sought to make history with a double catch of its reusable rocket.
Starship Flight 15 is expected to orbit the Earth about 14 times over the course of 22 hours, before the company catches the rocket at its launchpad at Starbase, in south Texas .
The rocket itself was composed of two elements: the lower booster, with 33 raptor engines that fired off during takeoff, and the Starship at the top.
SpaceX had planned for both components to return to its tower, but the booster, named Super Heavy, was aborted and splashed down in the sea. The cause of that diversion remains unknown.
The Starship continued on sailing through space.
SpaceX has launched a flurry of test flights in recent years, as its chief executive Elon Musk pushes his vision of taking humans into space.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia approaches Arm CEO Haas as employees seek Huang's return, reports say
articles.title_zh: Nvidia approaches Arm CEO Haas as employees seek Huang's return, reports say
articles.content_orig:
President Trump suggested on Thursday that Tim Cook, former CEO of Apple, should become the leader of chip maker Nvidia following its chief executive Jensen Huang ’s resignation over his alleged affairs with two women.
“NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend! ” Trump posted on TruthSocial.
Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO on Thursday morning, in the wake of reports that he had allegedly been involved in two affairs, including one with a woman identified by U.S. intelligence as a Chinese spy.
It is unclear if Trump has reached out to Cook regarding this suggestion. TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.
Huang and the White House have maintained a close relationship since the start of Trump’s second term. During his official visit to China in May, Trump invited Huang to attend the summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The New York Times reported that the President insisted on inviting Huang to join the delegation despite concerns over Huang’s relationship with a woman who is believed to be a Chinese spy.
Speaking with reporters on Monday, Trump repeatedly downplayed Huang’s alleged affair, insisting that he believed the tech billionaire’s assertion that he knew nothing about the alleged espionage operation.
“I really believe him,” Trump told reporters during the White House press conference. “I think that he’ll be in good shape.”

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo makes emotional return to his ‘beloved diocese of Chiclayo’
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo makes emotional return to his ‘beloved diocese of Chiclayo’
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo has made an emotional return to his former diocese of Chiclayo in Peru, where large crowds welcomed their former bishop exactly one month after he had lung cancer surgery, and he thanked them for their support during his recovery.
“As I look at your faces, a prayer of thanksgiving to the Lord arises in my heart for the blessing you have been and continue to be in my life,” he said.
About 500,000 people gathered for Mass at Pampas de Pimentel, a desert park just outside of Peru’s fourth-largest city, according to estimates from the Vatican, while another million lined his motorcade route.
Before he was elected pope, Leo had spent about two decades working in Peru as a missionary priest and served as bishop of Chiclayo, where he is still known as “Padre Roberto” and where his image is ubiquitous, from 2015 to 2023.
In Chiclayo, a coastal city of about 620,000, Leo earned a reputation for staying close to poor communities during times of crisis, including when the region was hit with devastating floods and the COVID-19 pandemic.
Some had camped overnight to see him, while others walked in the hot sun to avoid bumper-to-bumper traffic to get to the open-air Mass.
As he rode in his popemobile, people in the crowd waved yellow and white Vatican flags and shouted, “The pope is from Chiclayo.”
“What a joy it is to return to Chiclayo,” said Leo at the start of his homily.
Originally from Chicago and formerly known as Robert Francis Prevost, Leo also holds Peruvian citizenship and declared the country his homeland on Wednesday.
Peru is the final stop of his 12-day, three-country South America tour, coming after visits to Argentina and Uruguay. Approximately 12 million people have come to see him at public events so far.
Last month, he underwent surgery for lung cancer, amid fears that the trip would have to be cancelled. But doctors have said the cancer was localised, had not spread, and would not require further treatment .
Leo will stay in the Chiclayo area until Sunday, leading eight events, including a private dinner with the priests he oversaw during his time as bishop.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Nvidia Slides Again as Investors Brace for More Fallout; Nasdaq Slumps— Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Nvidia Slides Again as Investors Brace for More Fallout; Nasdaq Slumps— Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia investors turned bearish before this week's Jensen Huang saga. But the selling on Wall Street accelerated in the past few days, sending the stock to its sixth straight weekly drop, the longest losing streak since 2012.
The chip giant, which spent most of the year as the world's most valuable company, has lost 30% of its value during the losing streak. That's a drop of roughly $1.7 trillion in market cap and it pushed the company below Apple .
Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and led it for 33 years, resigned on Thursday after two separate extramarital affairs — one with an alleged Chinese spy and the other with an employee — were made public. The board named finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO while it conducts a search for a full-time successor.
Nvidia shares fell 13% this week, the most since April 2025. News of the first reported affair hit the front pages over the weekend, when Huang sent a letter to employees apologizing for being "unfaithful to my wife." The board convened late Wednesday after The New York Times reported on the other affair , this one with the company's vice president of health care.
By early Thursday morning, Huang was out, capping a stunning fall for the Nvidia co-founder, who had emerged as one of President Donald Trump's top allies in the corporate world.
"With the unfortunate departure of CEO Jensen Huang we expect a challenging transition for NVIDIA over the next few months," Gil Luria, an analyst at D.A. Davidson, wrote in a report on Thursday. Luria lowered his price target to $200 from $300, but maintained his buy rating. "We believe the market has appropriately adjusted for this transition," he wrote.
Last week, prior to Huang's departure, Nvidia shares dropped about 9%. Much of the decline came after the midterm elections, which resulted in sweeping victories for Democrats and the passage of dozens of ballot measures that could slow the artificial intelligence buildout.
In the weeks before the election, Nvidia's stock was sliding alongside the rest of the AI trade on concerns that rising interest rates would punish debt-heavy companies. While Nvidia is wildly profitable, big customers like neoclouds are reliant on the debt markets.
Heading into next week, the pressure is on Kress. Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday. Analysts are projecting 91% year-over-year revenue growth to $108.9 billion, according to LSEG. That's up 18-fold from the same quarter in 2022, just before OpenAI launched ChatGPT and kicked off the generative AI era.
Analysts at Oppenheimer wrote in a report on Thursday that, even though they see the company reporting solid earnings, "we expect fundamentals to take a backseat near term."
"The departure of Mr. Huang could, in our view, translate to a lingering share overhang," they wrote.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft outage shows the risks of relying on a single technology provider for essential services
articles.title_zh: Microsoft outage shows the risks of relying on a single technology provider for essential services
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft issued an apology Friday for a wide-ranging outage that shut down Outlook and other Microsoft 365 products, as the company worked to restore service nearly 24 hours after connectivity problems began.
"We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously," a Microsoft spokesperson said Friday. "We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services."
In a statement, Microsoft said the connectivity disruption stemmed from "an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade." The software giant said the underlying cause of the outage had been addressed and that they were still working to restore services to some customers.
Engineers scrambled to solve connectivity problems that began shortly before 1 p.m. ET on Thursday.
Email and calendar service Outlook, along with multiple Microsoft 365 services such as Sharepoint and Copilot, were largely down during the morning hours in the U.S. on Friday and throughout the Asian and European business days. Numerous external services that connect with Microsoft products were also hit. Users began to regain access to email and other services Friday morning.
In an update around 10:30 a.m. ET, Microsoft noted "encouraging recovery progress" and said that "service availability and email delivery performance [was] improving across a growing portion of affected infrastructure" as Outlook and other Microsoft 365 tools began to come back online.
In an earlier update Friday morning, Microsoft said that email queues were "approaching normal levels," but that intermittent issues were expected as recovery efforts continue. It had previously given updates by region, with Asia Pacific services among the first to start normalizing.
Engineering teams have been taking affected systems offline for fixes and bringing them back online gradually stages. They are prioritizing efforts to preserve emails delayed during the recovery process and reduce email queues and backlogs, extending the timeout window, whereby delayed emails continue to attempt delivery, to 48 hours to help protect messages.
Microsoft says it has not detected any malicious activity causing the outage, which it initially blamed on a traffic surge in part of its infrastructure and issues with a component responsible for processing server health. The company said it would issue a full report once its assessment of the outage was complete.
The company said in its initial updates on Thursday that the connectivity problems related to infrastructure "elevated load across multiple regions," caused by a "number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure." Some servers were failing automated health checks, it said.
Microsoft shares traded largely flat Friday.
Governments and businesses across the U.S., Asia-Pacific and Europe said they were monitoring the situation, which was causing widespread disruption.
The U.K.'s National Health Service said the outage was affecting some of its services but that patients should attend appointments as normal. Calls "may be subject to long waits" as a result of disruption to the organization, a hospital group serving South West London and the English county of Surrey said on X.
Earnings for Swiss luxury goods giant Richemont were slightly delayed on Friday due to the outage. Electric truck maker Workhorse Group, which was expected to report third-quarter results on Nov. 12, rescheduled the release to Nov. 16, citing business disruptions caused by the global Microsoft outage.
U.S. Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., told CNBC's "The Exchange" that he asked for a briefing on the outage. Gottheimer worked at Microsoft prior to serving in Congress.
"Is there something that went on that's nefarious here, or is this just something else? These outages occur in a lot of the companies, but the size of it and the length of it and the timing of it," Gottheimer said.
Air India said it had "temporarily rerouted" emails so it could continue to receive customer messages, adding that its flight operations were not affected.
Australian Home Affairs and Cyber Security Minister Tony Burke said in a press conference that Microsoft "believe they are dealing in some ways similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry," Reuters reported.
A fault with an update issued by cybersecurity company CrowdStrike caused one of the world's biggest IT system outages in 2024 , hitting airlines, banks and more.
Microsoft reported in 2025 that Copilot, its collection of AI assistants and tools, had more than 100 million monthly active users.
The incident highlights a business "resilience and dependency issue that has been decades in the making," James Owen, managing partner of Digital Risks at consultancy Control Risks, said by phone.
"We have become, organizationally in the private sector and more broadly, increasingly dependent on a smaller segment of technology and infrastructure as critical to daily life and business activities."
"Organizations are becoming more aware through a geopolitical lens about what technologies they adopt, whether their services are provided by firms in the U.S., or China, or elsewhere, but this shows the importance of proper recovery planning in the case of an IT outage. That could be manual backups, protocols that do not require internet connection, investing in diverse suppliers and crisis management planning rehearsals," he said.
Amazon Web Services and Google users also reported outages on the site on Thursday.
Amazon wrote on X that services were "operating normally" and an "unrelated disruption elsewhere on the internet is prompting some inaccurate news reports." The company referred users to its health dashboard for "accurate data."
At 4 p.m. ET Thursday, Microsoft said it had "validated an alternative service health check method" that brought some affected servers back online.
"We're now applying this change more broadly," Microsoft wrote. "We're also preparing automated recovery systems to continually detect and restart unresponsive servers, to maintain service stability while this change progresses."

articles.title_zh: Silverado's Dmitri Alperovitch on what's ahead for U.S.-China trade after Nvidia revelations
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure hasn't produced a broad shock to the credit market, but it is putting the company's role as a financier of artificial intelligence infrastructure under scrutiny.
Huang, who stepped down Thursday amid an espionage and adultery scandal, built Nvidia into an AI powerhouse in the 33 years since he co-founded the company. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO as the company searches for a permanent chief executive.
Nvidia not only supplies its graphics processing units to hyperscalers and tech giants, it also provides financing to other companies to help the industry expand. That could all change.
"Although we expect the company to fulfill all of its previously announced commitments, we believe that going forward, it may be more difficult for the company to negotiate new multi-party investments among ecosystem partners at the same scale it has done up to this point," Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider said in a note Thursday.
The news of Huang's resignation comes after investors were already concerned about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.
Tech bond yields have risen and spreads have widened on credit default swaps, most notably in lower-rated names. Credit default swaps are contracts in which investors pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. Wider spreads indicate investors view the bonds as riskier.
On Friday, the yield on Nvidia's 4.5% bond due in 2031 sat at 5.717%, nearly 5% higher week to date. Bond yields move inversely to prices.
Tech stocks slumped Friday with the Nasdaq 100 closing down 1.2% as markets continued to digest the Nvidia news. Yields on hyperscaler bonds ticked slightly higher on Friday, signaling the broader concern about AI debt  lingers.
It's the smaller AI companies that could ultimately see an impact if Nvidia makes any changes to its AI financing. The company had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, according to its last quarterly financial filing in July.
Neoclouds CoreWeave , Nebius and IREN are all in Nvidia's portfolio. Their shares were down sharply Thursday.
CoreWeave, which has become the poster child for AI debt fears, saw its bond yields retreat after its quarterly earnings on Tuesday eased investor concerns. The yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 was 14.79% on Friday after climbing to 16.7% last week. The spread on its five-year CDS also dropped more than 17% week to date, although it remained above 1,000 — which is generally considered a sign of distress.
It remains unclear how Nvidia's support for those companies may change, said CreditSights analyst Andy Li.
"We don't know what the ultimate strategy for Nvidia is going to be coming out the other side," he said.
"However, I think directionally, just given the fact that Jensen was so crucial in selling the Nvidia story and being a very aggressive deal maker, it's likely that a lot of this creative deal-making and circular financing and equity and credit support is going to moderate," he added.
CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC Wednesday , before Huang's departure, that Nvidia "is not one person."
"There are thousands of people over there that interface with thousands of people at my company every day. They integrate on the technology. They integrate on the physical infrastructure. They integrate on the networking," he said in an interview with "Squawk on the Street." "They have been a great partner for us for years. They will continue to be a great partner for us."
Bob Lang, founder and chief strategist at Explosive Options, doesn't see any big changes in terms of Nvidia's relevance or its ability to finance for now. As CFO, Kress was involved in the financing deals, and the search for a permanent CEO is going to take some time, he noted.
The real issue is just how much money the company will want to lend for AI financing, rather than, say using its hundreds of billions in free cash flow for other purposes, like share buybacks, capex, or acquisitions.
"Big companies like Nvidia and Meta, they're holding all the cards," he said. "When they decide that the game is over, that's it — it's going to be curtains for some of these smaller companies."
— CNBC'S Kif Leswing and Isabel O'Brien contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Investors Warn Bond Rout Isn’t Over After Week of Soaring Yields
articles.title_zh: Investors Warn Bond Rout Isn’t Over After Week of Soaring Yields
articles.content_orig:
The 10-year Treasury yield stayed over 5% on Friday after October's producer price index , a measure of wholesale prices, came in slightly less than expected.
The yield — the key benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — rose 4 basis points to 5.143%. It reached a high of 5.174% earlier in the day.
The 2-year Treasury note yield, typically more sensitive to short-term Federal Reserve interest rate decisions, was lower by less than 1 basis point at 4.859%. The longer-dated 30-year Treasury bond yield, sensitive to geopolitical risks, was more than 4 basis points higher at 5.472%.
One basis point equals 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
October's producer price index rose 0.3% versus September, less than the 0.4% expected by economists polled by Dow Jones. But on an annual basis, PPI rose 6.5% over the past 12 months, the biggest annual increase since November 2022.
There was "no silver lining" in the inflation report, said Chris Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS, adding that core PPI — which excludes  food, energy and trade services — increased 0.5% in October.
"It is economics 101 that producer prices lead consumer prices and right now it looks like consumers will be on the hook for a fresh burst of factory inflation," he said.
The moves come after 10-year Treasury yields jumped more than 13 basis points to more than 5% in Thursday's session , with the 2-year yield soaring more than 15 basis points.
Investors now see a Federal Reserve rate hike next month as a certainty. Traders are pricing in 100% odds of a rise at the Dec. 9 meeting, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. Odds of a quarter percentage point hike now stand at 89%, with the chance of a half point increase at around 14%.
Energy inflation remains a key part of the puzzle, with oil posting its second weekly decline as prospects of renewed strikes by the U.S. against Iran fade. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for December delivery were down 0.2% at $88.56 per barrel. Brent crude , the international oil benchmark, was higher by 0.02% at $95.84.

The Nasdaq Composite fell on Friday as Nvidia shares added to their recent losses, though the index still notched a winning week alongside the other two major averages.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq dropped 0.91% to 25,136.27, while the S&P 500 slid 0.4% to 7,561.67. The Dow Jones Industrial Average eked out a gain of 50.46 points, or 0.1%, to end at 52,347.55.
Equities initially popped after October's producer price index reading — a measure of wholesale inflation — showed an increase of 0.3% on the month. Economists polled by Dow Jones had seen headline PPI rising 0.4%.
However, the report also showed producer prices gaining 6.5% from 12 months earlier — the biggest annual advance since November 2022.
Nvidia shares weighed on the broader market for another day. The stock fell 2% Friday, extending the more than 4% drop it saw in the previous session. The pressure came after the exit of the scandal-hit chipmaker's founder and CEO Jensen Huang.
HSBC downgraded the chipmaker Friday to hold, believing that the stock will languish until the company lays out a permanent succession plan.
Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress , who's worked at the company for more than a decade, will lead the chipmaker as interim CEO. The company's board is looking both internally and externally for a full-time replacement for Huang.
Thomas Martin of Globalt Investments expects the process of finding a new CEO to "take a lot of time" and spur even more uncertainty for the name.
"What will happen to those types of financing arrangements, and will there be less of them just going forward or will there actually be unwinding of them?" the senior portfolio manager told CNBC. "What are the relationships going to be with their suppliers and with their customers? It's just early days."
The Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq all pulled back on Thursday after Huang stepped down from his post following reported extramarital affairs , including a relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believe is a Chinese spy. Analysts told CNBC that Huang's exit could trigger a 20% correction in the stock.
To be sure, Baird's Ross Mayfield believes a lot of pain has already been priced into the stock, though he still anticipates volatility ahead. More broadly, he expects to see investors continue to rotate into non-AI corners of the market independent of the latest developments with Nvidia.
"Even before all of this came out, and even before the election, chip stocks had been under pressure. There had already been worries about a blue wave — worries about a Democratic sweep — [and] worries about the [return on investment] on all of this capex," the investment strategist said. "It hasn't really changed the broad tenor of the market."
Even with the latest bout of market turbulence, the major averages notched weekly advances. The Nasdaq added 2.3%, while the S&P 500 rose 2.5%. The Dow gained 2.1%. All three indexes scored their best weekly performances since early August.
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite finished in negative territory on Friday.
The broad market index fell 0.4% to 7,561.67, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq shed 0.91% to 25,136.27.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average outperformed, rising 50.46 points, or 0.1%, to 52,347.55.
Jensen Huang's exit from Nvidia is scrambling the tech landscape as investors try to gauge the fallout for chip makers, neoclouds, and others in the artificial intelligence arms race.
The market has quickly passed judgement — bidding up shares of chipmakers like Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom while pushing down neoclouds such as Coreweave and AI server maker Dell Technologies .
Traders can benefit from the volatility, but the market has a tendency to overshoot in both directions and estimates are changing rapidly. Long-term investors may want to wait until the dust settles.

"The margin outlook and upgrade was better-than-expected with CSCO demonstrating strong operating leverage, though growing hyperscale revenue mix may be headwinds to gross margin in F2H27," he said.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia is done with Jensen Huang. The fallout in Washington is just beginning
articles.title_zh: Nvidia is done with Jensen Huang. The fallout in Washington is just beginning
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang is out at Nvidia. Washington is just getting started with him and the company he co-founded.
Huang, the leather-jacket-clad CEO of the world's most important chipmaker, resigned from Nvidia on Thursday after revelations that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy . But the spy saga is gripping Washington, and lawmakers are preparing for investigations into how the now-ex-CEO's affair may have damaged U.S. artificial intelligence dominance, the national security implications and the executive's close relationship with President Donald Trump and his Cabinet.
Republicans will have their chance first during their last six weeks controlling both chambers of Congress. GOP leaders immediately summoned Huang to Capitol Hill and said they would subpoena him if he doesn't agree to show up. In January, Democrats, who are already eager to make their mark with oversight when they take over the U.S. House and Senate, will be in the driver's seat.
"In this environment where there's some really high stakes when it comes to our national security, I would expect there would be some follow-up, yeah," Senate Majority Leader John Thune , R-S.D., told reporters at the Capitol on Thursday.
Huang and the woman with whom he reportedly had a relationship, Alice Huang, an executive at the Singaporean technology company Megaspeed and an alleged Chinese spy have drawn congressional attention. And Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has drawn fire after reports this week that he stalled President Donald Trump' s crackdowns on firms routing Nvidia chips to China .
Some Congress members have also called for an investigation into the role of the Bureau of Industry and Security, a subagency of the Commerce Department that manages and enforces export controls, in the Huang scandal.
The New York Times reported on Monday that Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, claimed in emails to Commerce investigators probing Alice Huang's company that he'd been in touch with Jeffrey Kessler, who leads BIS. The Commerce investigation into Megaspeed, which allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China, was then transferred to the Justice Department.
By Thursday night, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick t o testify before his committee in December. Later that same night, Lutnick had "proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions," Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement.
Scott threatened to subpoena Huang if he does not appear. A banking panel spokesperson did not immediately respond Friday morning when asked if they'd heard from Huang.
"Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology," Scott wrote to Huang. "The American people deserve answers."
And with Democrats poised to take control of both chambers come January, the tech mogul's close ties to the White House will add fuel to an already burning fire as the new majority spools up myriad investigations into the Trump administration.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer , D-N.Y., in a post to X on Thursday, said "Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk."  Schumer is in a contested race to become Senate majority leader in the next Congress.
The senators who will lead those investigations, and hold subpoena power in the new Congress, are gearing up for Nvidia to take center stage.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., the likely incoming chair of the Senate banking panel, said in a statement  Thursday that "Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and NVIDIA's board of directors still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls
Warren and Sen. Chris Coons , D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter Wednesday to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China."
Even before Democrats take control in January, Huang is expected to appear before Congress.
House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast , R-Fla., is actively negotiating for Huang to testify before House committees and told reporters Thursday the Nvidia CEO has agreed to appear in the coming weeks.
Details of that testimony are still being worked out, Mast said. It would likely include his committee, as well as the House intelligence panel and the House Permanent Select Committee on China, and it would be under oath and transcribed. It's not clear at this point whether it would be public.
"We want to see him basically in a week … Sooner rather than later," Mast told reporters Thursday, adding that he believed it would happen before Thanksgiving.
If Huang doesn't willingly appear, Mast said he will subpoena him.
Mast, along with House Select China Committee Chair Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., and House Intelligence Committee Chair Rep. Rick Crawford, R-Ark., sent a second request Thursday to Huang and Teter  requesting they appear and giving them an 8 p.m. ET Friday deadline to respond. Mast also sent a second request to Kessler.
Rep. Josh Gottheimer , D-N.J., a member of the House Intelligence Committee, said Friday during an appearance on CNBC's "The Exchange" that he wants answers from Huang on the national security and export implications of the affair.
"From an intelligence committee perspective, you can imagine from an AI perspective, how important this is for our national security, for our critical infrastructure and understand when it comes to chip policy, what exactly got to China and ... did Megaspeed divert chips?" Gottheimer said.
The calls for immediate investigation into Huang and Nvidia on the day of his resignation represent a stunning fall from grace in the halls of power for the former CEO. Huang was one of the most effective voices for the AI industry in Washington — able to toggle between leveraging his relationship with Trump and defending his industry from fears about AI's risks to lawmakers.
"He is always the TED Talk guy," one senior Democratic staff member who was granted anonymity to describe private meetings they had attended with Huang, told CNBC. "He's really good and articulate, and really good at explaining why AI is important and why it's so important for the United States to be leading here."
The staffer said Huang was a "happy warrior" for AI, and stayed longer than scheduled or anticipated for questions from lawmakers. But in the meetings with lawmakers the aide attended, they said Huang did not aggressively push against export controls or get too "deep in the weeds" to really "lobby one way or the other" with the lawmakers.
Huang has repeatedly resisted export controls publicly, a move that has rubbed some lawmakers the wrong way.
Some lawmakers even lamented the loss of Huang, despite the inevitable buzzsaw he now faces on Capitol Hill.
"It's just sad all around," Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., said of Huang's resignation.

HSBC downgraded the chipmaker Friday to hold, believing that the stock will languish until the company lays out a permanent succession plan.
Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress , who's worked at the company for more than a decade, will lead the chipmaker as interim CEO. The company's board is looking both internally and externally for a full-time replacement for Huang.
Thomas Martin of Globalt Investments expects the process of finding a new CEO to "take a lot of time" and spur even more uncertainty for the name.
"What will happen to those types of financing arrangements, and will there be less of them just going forward or will there actually be unwinding of them?" the senior portfolio manager told CNBC. "What are the relationships going to be with their suppliers and with their customers? It's just early days."
The Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq all pulled back on Thursday after Huang stepped down from his post following reported extramarital affairs , including a relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believe is a Chinese spy. Analysts told CNBC that Huang's exit could trigger a 20% correction in the stock.
To be sure, Baird's Ross Mayfield believes a lot of pain has already been priced into the stock, though he still anticipates volatility ahead. More broadly, he expects to see investors continue to rotate into non-AI corners of the market independent of the latest developments with Nvidia.
"Even before all of this came out, and even before the election, chip stocks had been under pressure. There had already been worries about a blue wave — worries about a Democratic sweep — [and] worries about the [return on investment] on all of this capex," the investment strategist said. "It hasn't really changed the broad tenor of the market."
Even with the latest bout of market turbulence, the major averages notched weekly advances. The Nasdaq added 2.3%, while the S&P 500 rose 2.5%. The Dow gained 2.1%. All three indexes scored their best weekly performances since early August.
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite finished in negative territory on Friday.
The broad market index fell 0.4% to 7,561.67, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq shed 0.91% to 25,136.27.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average outperformed, rising 50.46 points, or 0.1%, to 52,347.55.
Jensen Huang's exit from Nvidia is scrambling the tech landscape as investors try to gauge the fallout for chip makers, neoclouds, and others in the artificial intelligence arms race.
The market has quickly passed judgement — bidding up shares of chipmakers like Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom while pushing down neoclouds such as Coreweave and AI server maker Dell Technologies .
Traders can benefit from the volatility, but the market has a tendency to overshoot in both directions and estimates are changing rapidly. Long-term investors may want to wait until the dust settles.
CNBC Pro subscribers can read more here .
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure hasn't produced a broad shock to the credit market, but it is putting the company's role as a financier of artificial intelligence infrastructure under scrutiny.
Huang, who stepped down Thursday amid an espionage and adultery scandal, built Nvidia into an AI powerhouse in the 33 years since he co-founded the company. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO as the company searches for a permanent chief executive.
Nvidia not only supplies its graphics processing units to hyperscalers and tech giants, it also provides financing to other companies to help the industry expand. That could all change.
"Although we expect the company to fulfill all of its previously announced commitments, we believe that going forward, it may be more difficult for the company to negotiate new multi-party investments among ecosystem partners at the same scale it has done up to this point," Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider said in a note Thursday.
Apple shares climbed nearly 1% Friday, reaching an intraday record of $360.80, lifting the company's market value above $5.2 trillion.
The stock has benefited as investors move away from companies exposed to the AI infrastructure boom.
While many of its Magnificent Seven peers are committed to AI infrastructure buildouts, Apple has managed to stay away from the costly AI arms race. Bernstein analysts recently called Apple a "safe haven " and reiterated an outperform rating on Apple in the report, and a $380 price target, implying about 7% upside from Thursday's close.
Check out CNBC's live blog here to read more about the stocks making big moves on Friday.
— Darla Mercado and Ananya Chetia
Cisco topped estimates on fiscal first-quarter earnings on Thursday, but Wall Street analysts are still somewhat measured on the outlook for the make of networking technologies amid the AI boom.
Tim Long at Barclays maintained his equal-weight rating on the stock in a Friday note, with a price target of $109 and potential upside of 6.9%.
"One area of weakness in the quarter was that hyperscaler AI orders were likely down meaningfully Q/Q in FQ1 based on our estimates, but these orders tend to be lumpy," he said.
Michael Ng at Goldman Sachs has a neutral rating on the stock, noting an "orders miss," per a Nov. 12 note.
"The margin outlook and upgrade was better-than-expected with CSCO demonstrating strong operating leverage, though growing hyperscale revenue mix may be headwinds to gross margin in F2H27," he said.
Nvidia is going to struggle until it gets a new CEO to permanently replace Jensen Huang and take over from CFO-turned-interim-CEO Colette Kress, according to HSBC.
Analyst Frank Lee downgraded the chipmaker to hold from buy. His price target of $170, down from $365, implies upside of just 2.3% from Thursday's close.
"We believe the uncertainties will prevail until a permanent succession plan is laid out and the new CEO is able to demonstrate execution capabilities," Lee said in a Friday note to clients.
CNBC Pro subscribers can read more here .
Bitcoin traded below $70,000 for the first time since August in a risk-off move, falling as low as $67,632.68, its lowest level since Aug. 19, according to Coin Metrics.
Its recent weakness coincides with strength in the U.S. dollar. On Friday, the dollar index reached its highest level since April 2025, following hotter-than-expected inflation earlier this week that increased expectations of further Fed tightening, pushing Treasury yields and the dollar higher while pressuring both bitcoin and gold – despite their appeal as alternative stores of value in the longer term.
Throughout November, bitcoin has been struggling from the combination of dollar strength, institutional selling and, this week, more than $1 billion in leveraged bitcoin liquidations, per CoinGlass. The declines began in late October, as concerns over AI valuations and spending fueled a broad tech sell-off, and were compounded by the $6.3 billion Binance hack and weakening institutional ETF demand.

articles.content_orig:
By WILIAM HUNTER, SENIOR SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY REPORTER
Published: 07:01 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 11:58 EST, 13 November 2026
If you are reading this, congratulations – you have survived the end of the world.
That is if a 1960 study predicting today to be ‘doomsday’ is to be believed – although with the Microsoft outage hitting offices, your day may still be a scene of panicked chaos as operations grind to a disastrous halt.
Conspiracy-minded commenters on social media have found a striking connection between the global disruption and a theory claiming ‘doomsday’ will occur on November 13, 2026.
One user cheekily suggested: 'Is it a mere coincidence? I don't think so... it was all planned.'
Written by Heinz von Foerster, an Austrian-American cybernetics expert, and two of his students, the study examined the last 2,000 years of human population growth and predicted it would ‘approach infinity’ and annihilate itself.
Writing in the journal Science, the trio argued: 'Our great-great-grandchildren will not starve. They will be squeezed to death.'
And with the supposed date of the apocalypse in mind, many commenters have pointed to their lack of emails as an ominous portent of doom.
Social media users have found a striking connection between this wacky prediction and the recent Microsoft outage
A doomsday event was predicted for today, Friday, November 13, 2026, by three scientists in 1960. Today, Microsoft servers are undergoing a global outage. Is it a mere coincidence? I don't think so .. it was all planned.
People have flocked to social media to share their wild conspiracy theories connecting the Microsoft outage to today's supposed apocalypse.
On X, one quipped: 'Is this the Doomsday November 13th that we all were talking about? @Microsoft.'
While another added: 'In 1960, scientists used a mathematical equation to predict that Friday, November 13, 2026 would be Doomsday. Nobody believed them until Outlook crashed globally this morning.'
Meanwhile, some conspiracy lovers made the connection to the traditionally unlucky date of Friday 13, as well as some other even stranger speculations.
One commenter wrote: 'It's Friday the 13th. Microsoft outage means no email. These seem related.'
While another asked: 'If astrology isn't real then why is the Microsoft outage happening on the last day of Mercury Retrograde?'
In reality, Professor von Foerster's theory has long since been debunked and doesn't have the slightest connection to today's internet outages.
In 1960, one of the world's leading scientific journals published a paper suggesting that the population would surge toward infinity (illustrated), leading to 'doomsday' on Friday, November 13, A.D. 2026
So Doomsday was predicted back in 1960s for November 13th 2026. And all of a sudden Microsoft down. Summin ain’t adding up 🧐 https://t.co/rGvIjLwR4v
Professor Alan MacEachern, a professor of history at Western University, pointed out that the 1960 calculations were based on a fundamental error.
Writing in The Conversation, he noted that the global birth rate is now significantly lower than it was when the article was published.
This suggests the prediction of doomsday on November 13 is based on outdated figures.
‘Only around 1993 did that accuracy begin to falter and the global population began falling behind the forecasts,’ Professor MacEachern explained.
‘Today, the global birth rate is slightly less than half the 1960 rate.’
That means there’s no need for anyone to worry about being ‘squeezed to death’.
Professor MacEachern also points out that the lead author, Heinz von Foerster, was a stage magician at one point in his life.
As a result, the scientist may have used elements of his tricks in his paper.
Microsoft users continued to experience disruption today as the tech giant worked to resolve outages impacting some of its most popular services
'Borrowing the classic language of stagecraft, an effective illusion relies on three parts: the setup, the extraordinary turn and the final reveal that returns the situation to normal,' Professor MacEachern explained.
'Von Foerster and his co–authors' article gained attention because it was an ordinary scientific article wrapped in an extraordinary title and conclusion.
'It retained significance because it was firmly grounded in research and argument.
'To draw the world's attention to a serious matter by way of absurdity — that's a good trick.'
That means there's no need for anyone to worry about being 'squeezed to death'.
On the other hand, the ongoing Microsoft outage appears to be related to an internal issue with the company's internal infrastructure.
In several notices posted on social media, Microsoft said it was investigating the disruptions and suggested the problems could be down to parts of its infrastructure 'experiencing elevated load'.
Microsoft determined a number of servers failed during automated health checks and that its alternatives to bring those servers back online were not immediately taking effect.
Likewise, experts have ruled out the possibility of a cyber-attack disrupting the tech giant's services.
Mantas Sasnauskas, cyber-security researcher and editor-in-chief of Ransomnews , told the Daily Mail: 'Nothing so far points to a cyberattack. Microsoft says it is not aware of any malicious activity, and what it has described fits that.
'Servers dropped out and then failed again as soon as traffic came back. A denial-of-service attack looks like a flood of hostile traffic. This looks like a failure inside the platform.'
However, as Microsoft battles to bring systems back online, the company has acknowledged that efforts to restore services were 'not taking as expected'.
Millions of users around the world began reporting that Outlook was down shortly after 6pm GMT on Thursday, in what experts have dubbed the 'most disruptive email-related business outage of all time'.
More than 14 hours later, users are still unable to open their inboxes, send emails and access other Microsoft services.
Governments, police forces and numerous companies around the world have reported problems with their services, but no definitive cause has been given.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive / How Nvidia’s Jensen Huang – and Trump – jumped the guardrails
articles.title_zh: Exclusive / How Nvidia’s Jensen Huang – and Trump – jumped the guardrails
articles.content_orig:
In January, the general counsel for what was then the worldâs most valuable company delivered a blunt directive on chip export controls to more than a dozen government officials: What Donald Trump and his friend Jensen Huang want, goes.
âI was with the president when he and Jensen discussed this so I want to let you know what the president wanted,â said Nvidiaâs Tim Teter, according to people with access to a detailed account of the call. âHe wants this to go fast.âÂ
People on the call fell silent.
At issue were proposed conditions on licenses to export Nvidiaâs H200 chips to China, which included requirements that chipsellers know who their cloud customers were before shipping and conduct know-your-customer checks on any buyers purchasing more than a few thousand chips.
Nvidia objected, with Teter calling the cloud-customer requirement a âpoison pillâ for the company, the people said. Nvidia also wanted the threshold for the know-your-customer checks to be in the tens of thousands (the equivalent of billions of dollars of chips) and pushed for end-of-life conditions to only apply to chips that were facing export controls. While itâs not unusual for big corporations to work with US government agencies and Congressional staffers on legislation or agency rulemaking, or even to see draft regulation in advance, people familiar with Nvidia and its former CEOâs Washington connections say the chipmaker wielded an unprecedented level of influence in shaping guidelines with far-reaching global security and business implications for the entire industry. The previously unreported discussions have only taken on greater significance since Huang stepped down from the company he co-founded decades ago after media reports of extramarital affairs with two subordinates and one with a customer and suspected Chinese spy.
Nvidia declined to comment. Spokespeople for the White House didnât immediately respond to requests for comment.
A spokesperson for the Bureau of Industry and Security, which is housed within the Department of Commerce, said it was âcompletely routineâ for the department and other agencies to work with individual companies in this manner and that âoften the conditions change in response to legitimate commercial considerationsâ raised by corporations. The final version of all license conditions are reviewed by the state, defense, energy, and commerce departments.âNvidia would have gone through the same process for license conditions as any other license applicant. Nvidia consulting with non-political experts at multiple US government agencies regarding its proposed changes to the conditions is consistent with standard practice,â the spokesperson said.
If Trump was Huangâs friend in the White House, Teter was his muscle in Washington. After more than two decades at law firm Cooley LLP, Teter joined Nvidia in 2017, soon after the chipmaker announced the beginning of the â AI computing era .â Nvidiaâs GPUs had sparked the âbig bangâ of modern AI, Huang wrote at the time, years before Nvidia would turn into the worldâs most valuable company.
But as Nvidia became a bigger geopolitical force â and Huang became a fixture alongside Trump at meetings, dinners and the Oval Office â Huang and Teter developed a âscorched earth, adversarial attitude,â according to a former government official familiar with their Washington presence. âThey make things more personal, going after think tankers, government officials, and the like,â the former official said, referring to reports of Nvidia targeting critics of the company and proponents of export controls.
As he bulldozed through Washington, Teter regularly invoked President Trumpâs name to push Nvidiaâs agenda. In one exchange viewed by Semafor, Teter accused government officials who were developing export restrictions of misrepresenting Nvidiaâs products and President Trumpâs policies, chiding them for not carrying out Trumpâs agenda and insisting that Trump deserved their support. Teter and the team of Nvidia lobbyists would often capitalize on their implicit White House backing and on the fact that most Hill staffers didnât have the technical expertise to fight back on the companyâs claims that certain restrictions werenât technically feasible, even if later they were proven wrong, current and former congressional staffers told Semafor. Staffers âwere kind of just believing whatever they were told,â and Nvidia would get all sorts of bills watered down, one staffer said.
Nvidiaâs âMO has largely been gaslighting,â creating an âintense trust deficit between the government and the Hill and Nvidia,â a former staffer said. And âobviously, the canonical example at this point is Nvidia denyingâ improper chip sales to China, this person said.
Huang has said thereâs no evidence chips were getting diverted to China, but Bloomberg has reported that Nvidia undercounted the Megaspeed sales it reported to the US government by 50,000 chips, worth billions of dollars. Companies tied to Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese spy, have purchased at least $7.5 billion of Nvidia chips since 2023, The Information reported .
But well before Nvidia came under fire for its relationship with Megaspeed, Nvidia told staffers that a provision in the 2025 Chip Security Act, which would require chipmakers to be able to locate their chips, was a nonstarter. âThey basically said it was not technically feasibleâ the former staffer said, âthey were like, âwe would need completely new technology to do this, and even if we did it would be very easily spoofable.ââ
In meetings with committee staff, Nvidia lobbyists argued location verification would create security holes. They âran this line of bullsh-t on how the Chip Security Act was going to create all these cyber vulnerabilities,â a second former staffer said. âWe spent six months going behind them and having to unpack all of the bullsh-t that [they were] telling to other offices.â
Then in December, Reuters reported a new location verification technology feature, which Nvidia had been demonstrating privately for months. The feature was launched in May, meaning the company had been âlying to Congress about the technical feasibility while you were literally baking it into your next chip generation,â this person said.
Nvidia declined to comment on the location-verification technology.
Nvidia, though, found a willing partner in Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who appeared to be more concerned with avoiding another painful trade war with China, as Trump was, and with staying on the presidentâs good side than with combing through the innards of chip regulations, according to people familiar with the matter. âLutnick was fine with the H200s [being sold]. I think heâs just tried to be very careful to not rock the boat, and also itâs been convenient to make friends with industry allies like Jensen, especially since Trump likes Jensen as well,â a former Commerce official told Semafor.
A former State Department official told Semafor that officials were weighing whether to add Megaspeed, the company linked to Alice Huang, to a government blacklist as early as the spring of 2025, earlier than has been previously reported . âIf you really wanted to get someone on the entity list you could do it extremely fast if you want to,â the former Commerce Department official said.
Jensen Huang became one of the most powerful men in the world by churning out coveted chips and personally deciding who got what,and when. Computing power is the lifeblood of the AI industry, and Americaâs roughly nine-to-one compute advantage over China is the countryâs most durable edge in the AI race. As the leading purveyor of that compute, it was never in Huangâs interest to forgo the second largest chip market.
